Hi, all. I’ve been working on formalizing stability theory in model theory. And I require the conpect of Morley rank, which comes from Cantor-Bendixson analysis. So I first developed the core definitions and facts of this theory in my private project.

This development includes things like:

  • isolated points of a set
  • transfinite iterates of the derived-set operator
  • stabilization of the derived-set sequence
  • the perfect kernel
  • set-/point-level Cantor-Bendixson ranks and scatteredness

After that, I also mangeed to give a generalization of the Cantor-Bendixson decomposition theorem in mathlib (exists_countable_union_perfect_of_isClosed) for any topology and any cardinal. Now the entire module currently consists of more than 600 lines. While some proofs haven't been finely golfed or reorganized, a few helper lemmas might also be over-abstracted.

Before trying to upstream it, I wanted to ask whether this kind of material seems in scope for mathlib. It seems like fairly natural general-topology API around derived sets / perfect sets / scatteredness. However, as far as I know, it also seems not to have many important applications except for model theory and descriptive set theory. And I'm not an expert on this, so I will just let you guys to decide.

If this does seem appropriate, I’d then plan to split it into a few small stacked PRs rather than one large PR.

I’d appreciate feedback on:

  • whether this overall direction seems suitable for mathlib,
  • which parts seem clearly worth upstreaming first,
  • whether the API seems too bloat/heavy.

I also have a couple of more specific design questions:

  1. Some definitions were initially universe-polymorphic, but many of fundamental results use cardinality arguments, where I found it much more convenient to keep the ordinal universe aligned with the universe of the underlying type. In the end I give up universe polymorphism entirely. I’m not sure whether universe polymorphism is actually desirable here, and whether there is a standard way to preserve it while still carrying out the relevant cardinal arguments cleanly.
  2. For generalization, I specifically avoid adding extra assumptions on the topogoly, but as a result many of the basic or core statements end up requiring IsClosed hypotheses. I’m not sure whether this is the right level of generality, or whether there is a refined choice of definitions which does not rely on closedness assumptions without forcing stronger topological assumptions.

This all seems in scope for Mathlib. As the ordinal person around here I'll be glad to review your material :slight_smile:

re universe polymorphism: very often you can salvage that by using docs#Small. For instance, the Cantor-Bendixson rank of a Small.{u} topological space will be an Ordinal.{u}.
I'll skim your code and give you some feedback. Just one sec.
I'm not sure we need isolatedPoints as a separate def from derivedSet. We can just write (derivedSet s)ᶜ after all.

I see your definition of the iterated derived set makes use of limit recursion. As I like to say, you don't need limit recursion like 90% of the time. You can instead do something like this.

def iteratedDerivedSet (s : Set X) (o : Ordinal) : Set X :=
  if o = 0 then s else ⋂ a < o, derivedSet (iteratedDerivedSet s a)
That way you don't need to split up every single proof into three cases. Just two: zero, and everything else.
stayOn seems somewhat ad-hoc. Presumably what you want to say is Filter.EventuallyConst (iteratedDerivSet s) atTop?
Perhaps setCBRank could just be cantorBendixsonRank?

I believe that behaves differently on edge cases such as ℚ as a set in the natural topology of ℝ.

We want every definition in Mathlib to have good API. We could define isolatedPoints for a general set in a general topological space, and provide that API. But I worry that said API would just largely duplicate that for derivedSet. And at that point we're losing convenience, rather than gaining it.

How come? Wouldn't you just get iteratedDerivedSet s o = s for all o?

On successor ordinals, it's ℝ. On limit ordinals and zero, it's ℚ itself. But in your definition, it's ℝ except for zero.
Wait, is it not supposed to be that?
Nevermind, I see the issue.
Do we care about edge cases like these? Surely we only really care about the Cantor-Bendixson rank of closed sets.
The fact that under your definition the iterated derived sets switch between ℚ and ℝ at limit points seems like an artifact, rather than intended behavior.
I actually believe that the concept of Cantor-Bendixson rank is more like a prototype or the original motivation of transfinite recursion and ordinal.
It is :slight_smile: It's also why we call docs#Ordinal.deriv a derivative even when it has nothing to do with derivatives - the name comes from these derived sets.

Violeta Hernández ha dicho:

stayOn seems somewhat ad-hoc. Presumably what you want to say is Filter.EventuallyConst (iteratedDerivSet s) atTop?

In fact, why not prove ∀ a ≥ (succ #s).ord, sᵈ[a] = sᵈ[b] first, then define the perfect kernel as sᵈ[(succ #s).ord], and finally define the Cantor-Bendixson rank as sInf (iteratedDeriv s ⁻¹' perfectKernel s)?

Violeta Hernández 說：

Do we care about edge cases like these? Surely we only really care about the Cantor-Bendixson rank of closed sets.

I'm not sure. It seems that there is a better way to make this definition behave well on all sets in the most general topological setting. Just modify the definition of the derived set to be the subspace with its isolated points removed, rather than the set of its limit points.
So s ∩ derivedSet s instead of just derivedSet s?
That seems reasonable.
then my definition and yours agree :slight_smile:

Violeta Hernández 說：

Violeta Hernández ha dicho:

stayOn seems somewhat ad-hoc. Presumably what you want to say is Filter.EventuallyConst (iteratedDerivSet s) atTop?

In fact, why not prove ∀ a ≥ (succ #s).ord, sᵈ[a] = sᵈ[b] first, then define the perfect kernel as sᵈ[(succ #s).ord], and finally define the Cantor-Bendixson rank as sInf (iteratedDeriv s ⁻¹' perfectKernel s)?

Then you can only get perfect kernel and set-wise Cantor-Bendixson rank of a closed set, since the first statement holds for closed sets.
No, that statement should always work. If o ≠ 0 then iteratedDerivSet s o = iteratedDerivSet (closure s) o. So the theorem reduces to the case of a closed set.

In fact, do we really lose out on much if we define:

def iteratedDerivedSet (s : Set X) (o : Ordinal) : Set X :=
  if o = 0 then closure s else ⋂ a < o, derivedSet (iteratedDerivedSet s a)

It would let us remove a lot of IsClosed hypotheses, at the very least.

Violeta Hernández ha dicho:

No, that statement should always work. If o ≠ 0 then iteratedDerivSet s o = iteratedDerivSet (closure s) o. So the theorem reduces to the case of a closed set.

For a T1 space, I should say.
I would prefer to just use "relative" derived set in the definition.
But that will make perfect kernel be "relative" perfect as well, seemingly.
Well in that case, you should have iteratedDerivSet s o = s ∩ iteratedDerivSet (closure s) o, at least in a T1 space. So you still have the theorem that it's constant after (succ #s).ord.
If the space isn't T0, then you can have this situation: if x and y are topologically indistinguishable, then derivSet {x} = {y} and derivSet {y} = {x}. So the sequence is not eventually constant.

Violeta Hernández 說：

If the space isn't T0, then you can have this situation: if x and y are topologically indistinguishable, then derivSet {x} = {y} and derivSet {y} = {x}. So the sequence is not eventually constant.

It becomes empty on a limit ordinal, isn't it?
oh, yeah. or at step 2 under my definition. or at step 1 if we take the relative derived set.

in fact, if we take relative derived sets, then the sequence of iterated derived sets will always be antitone, then it must be eventually constant because you'd eventually run out of subsets otherwise
so you don't need the closure condition to define the CB rank. whether it means anything sensible outside of the closed case, that's another thing entirely.

Since these definitions are well-behaved and consistent on closed sets, what we are actually looking for is a reasonable fallback for undefined cases, similar to how Lean defines 1 / 0 = 0. So it seems reasonable to require an IsClosed hypothesis for these statements just as when you use a theorem about division like mul_inv_cancel, it requires a non-zero hypothesis.
you know, i don't actually think Mathlib has "a monotone/antitone function from Ordinal.{u} into a Small.{u} type is eventually constant"
it'd be nice to prove that
I'll PR later (unless you want to try and PR this yourself)
No, I’m happy to leave it to you since I believe you're more familiar with this part.

I see your definition of the iterated derived set makes use of limit recursion. As I like to say, you don't need limit recursion like 90% of the time. You can instead do something like this.

def iteratedDerivedSet (s : Set X) (o : Ordinal) : Set X :=

This seems to be an OrdinalApprox.gfpApprox esstentially, at least for closed sets or in a T1 space.

Violeta Hernández said:

It is :) It's also why we call docs#Ordinal.deriv a derivative even when it has nothing to do with derivatives - the name comes from these derived sets.

By a remarkable coincidence the Cantor-Bendixson derivative actually is almost a derivative in an algebraic sense.

Zikang 'Axi' Yu said:

However, as far as I know, it also seems not to have many important applications except for model theory and descriptive set theory.

I don't know if this would be pushing the generality too far, but in model theory we often (implicitly or explicitly) use various generalizations of the Cantor-Bendixson derivative where one removes some other kind of 'small' open set. For instance, you might fix a cardinality κ\kappaκ and remove the union of all open sets of cardinality less than κ\kappaκ at each stage.

How difficult do you think it would be to accommodate this kind of generalization?

For instance, you might fix a cardinality κ\kappaκ and remove the union of all open sets of cardinality less than κ\kappaκ at each stage.

Actually, that's exactly my motivation for formalizing Cantor-Bendixson analysis. This is essentially related to the connection between Cantor-Bendixson rank and Morley rank. I also know some statements in this setting for calculating CB rank.

For example, one useful statement for computing the CB rank is the following:

CB(p)=α+1CB(p)=\alpha+1CB(p)=α+1

iff there is a clopen neighborhood U containing p such that every q in U \ {p} has CB(q) <= α, and infinitely many q in U \ {p} have CB(q)=α.

Edit: It seems that I misunderstand your question. I think your < κ-open-set variant is a genuinely broader generalization than Morley rank, so I'm not sure yet whether my current setup is abstract enough to accommodate it. And I wonder what conclusions this setting can derive?
Opened a PR for the result on monotone functions #37344

Zikang 'Axi' Yu said:

And I wonder what conclusions this setting can derive?

Well so that particular version shows up in the analysis of superstable theories, but when I said that I was also thinking about the analysis of totally transcendental theories in continuous logic, where a somewhat technical metric variant of Morley rank is required.
I think it might be best to hold off on generalizing until we actually need the more general theorems.
And then, figure out if the API we have is similar enough to what the more general definition would have, or if it'd be better to create a new API altogether.
Can we make derivedSet an OrderHom and prove that iteratedDerivedSet s and gfpApprox (derivedSet) s agree on every ordinal? Then we can conclude almost everything we need from FixedPointApproximants.
That seems silly. Why not define iteratedDerivSet via gfpApprox?
Because they behave differently on non-closed sets. Under this definition, we obtain a well-behaved total function across all ordinals and sets, but with a possibly non-standard mathematical meaning.
The use of gfpApprox essentially reduces to the relative derived set operator discussed previously.
What we can instead do is define relDerivedSet : Set α →o Set α via relDerivedSet s = s ∩ derivedSet s, and then define iteratedDerivedSet as the gfpApprox of that.
Makes sense. I'd refactor it in this way.
Opened three PRs for the refactored iteratedDerivedSet using gfpApprox and some other upsteam results. See: 37374, 37375, 37376.
As my focus has shifted, for those interested, feel free to import the downstream results for the refactored APIs from my private repo.
